conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You're here today to get your third dose of high-dose methotrexate for your lymphoma. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m okay. A bit tired and weak, but that’s been going on. My mouth is still sore from the last round, but it’s getting better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the mucositis can take time to heal. We’ll keep managing that with mouth rinses and pain meds. You’re scheduled for the methotrexate infusion tomorrow. Today, we’ll run some labs and give you IVIG for your immune deficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I had that last time, right? The IVIG?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every three weeks. We’ll give you 40 grams today with Tylenol and Benadryl first to prevent reactions. Any allergies we should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to penicillin, sulfa, morphine, omeprazole, and a few others. They’re all listed, I think.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we see that. We’ll avoid those. Your breathing and heart sounds look good on the chest X-ray. No fluid in the lungs. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I haven’t had any shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your kidney function closely during chemo. Methotrexate can affect the kidneys, so we’ll give you lots of fluids and check labs frequently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My sugars have been high lately. I know you’re watching that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood sugar was 219 today. At home you’re on metformin, and you say it’s under control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, between 80 and 160. But I eat better at home. Here, I’ve had some snacks—maybe too many crackers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain the higher readings. We may need insulin while you're here, but we’ll be cautious about low sugars, especially with your other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ll try to stick to the diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started your methotrexate infusion. Dose is 3.5 grams per square meter. You’re tolerating it well so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor for nausea, mouth sores, and kidney issues. You’ll get leucovorin later to help clear the drug. We expect you to clear it within 48 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your methotrexate levels are dropping well—0.31 yesterday, now 0.04. That means your body is clearing the drug as expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good. It means lower risk of toxicity. Your weakness from the brain lymphoma is also improving, which is a positive sign the treatment is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger than I did after the fall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned more abdominal pain and gas today. Given your history of bowel perforation, we did a KUB. No obstruction or free air—good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s crampy and I’m passing a lot of gas. My ostomy output is higher too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on clear liquids for now and send a stool test to check for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your first stool test came back negative for C. diff. But since symptoms continue, we’re repeating it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still hurts. I hope it’s not serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another X-ray shows no obstruction. But we’re concerned enough to do a CT scan today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my history?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with contrast. It will help us see if there’s inflammation or infection in the bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT is back. There’s wall thickening in your small bowel and some air outside the intestine. It’s likely infection or inflammation, not ischemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection? From what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat stool test just came in positive for C. difficile. That’s likely the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your medical history. But we’re starting oral vancomycin right away—125 mg four times a day for 14 days. That should clear it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will that affect my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve checked—no major interactions. We’ll keep monitoring your kidney and liver labs too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal pain is improving, and your ostomy output is coming down. That’s a good sign the vancomycin is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Still bloated, but less pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on vancomycin for the full course. Also, your blood sugar has been high—up to 497. We started Lantus insulin and adjusted your sliding scale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I ate those extra crackers. Won’t happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. But at home, if sugars stay high, you might need insulin long-term. We ordered an A1C, but it’s pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll watch my diet more carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your white count is low—2.0. We’re giving one dose of Neupogen to help boost it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s standard after chemo. It helps your body make white blood cells faster and lowers infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I give it myself at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you have the supplies. We’ll send one dose home with instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my dexamethasone? I’ve been on 2 mg twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re tapering it down to 1 mg twice a day. Since your brain swelling is better, we can reduce it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any side effects from lowering it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people feel tired or achy during taper, but we’ll monitor. It’s important to avoid sudden stops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain is gone, C. diff treatment is on track, and your lymphoma treatment was successful. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before, plus oral vancomycin for 12 more days. Dexamethasone is now 1 mg twice a day. And you’ll take Neupogen tonight if you have it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow-up appointment on ___ at 2:30 PM. You’ll also return for your next chemo admission on ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll mark it down. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on the clear diet until the vancomycin is done. Watch for fever, worsening pain, or diarrhea. Call us if any of those happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my mouth sores. Any new advice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using the magic mouthwash. They should continue improving. Hydration and soft foods help too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been drinking a lot of water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. That helps with both mucositis and kidney clearance of meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my ostomy? It’s still active.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s settling. As the infection clears, output should normalize. Keep the skin clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have supplies at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And remember, no NSAIDs—they can irritate your gut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I only take my prescribed pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re doing everything right. We’ll see you at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. The nurse will go over your discharge papers now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your CMV test came back negative. No active infection there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your immune system is challenged, so we check regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll let the team know you’re ready for discharge prep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Get some rest and take it easy at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you at your next appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.
